deciding quote: 'EXTRAORDINARY FACTS relating to the Vision of Colours ... BY MR. JOHN DALTON. READ OCT. 31st, 1794.' (p.28; paper runs pp.28-45)
source url: https://archive.org/details/memoirsofliterar05manc (Memoirs Lit & Phil Soc Manchester vol. 5 pt 1, 1798, scan + OCR text); Henry 1854 p.24: https://archive.org/details/memoirsoflifesci00henruoft
notes: Paper starts p.28 and ends p.45 (next paper begins p.46). Volume dated 1798. Henry p.24 independently: 'read before the Society, October 31, 1794, and is published, Vol. v. p. 28'. I used the archive.org scan of vol. 5 rather than the Commons DPLA files; same printing.

deciding quote: 'Born: September 5 or 6, 1766, Eaglesfield, Cumberland, England'
suggested wording: He was 28 when he read it (born September 1766).
notes: Age 28 on 31 Oct 1794 is right whichever birth date is used. Britannica gives 5 or 6 Sept, so do not print '6 Sep' as certain on screen.

deciding quote: Britannica: in 1793 he moved to Manchester 'to teach mathematics at a dissenting academy, the New College'. Lonsdale p.79: 'His first six years were engaged in the New College'
source url: https://www.britannica.com/biography/John-Dalton; https://archive.org/details/worthiescumberl02lonsgoog (Lonsdale, Worthies of Cumberland: John Dalton, preface dated 20 July 1874)
notes: Quaker: Britannica 'born into a Quaker family'; Henry and Lonsdale treat him as a lifelong Friend. Lonsdale p.79: appointed to the 'mathematical and natural philosophy course ... vacant in 1793'. Dalton's letters of 1793-94 are addressed 'At the New College, Manchester' (Lonsdale). So teaching there in Oct 1794 is supported.

deciding quote: archive.org record of vol. 1 pt 1: 'A new system of chemical philosophy ... Manchester : Printed by S. Russell ... 1808'; Britannica: 'a pioneer in the development of modern atomic theory'
notes: Vol. 1 part 1 is 1808; later parts 1810 and 1827. '1808' is right for the first appearance of the book.

deciding quote: 'The flower was pink, but it appeared to me almost an exact sky-blue by day; in candle-light, however, it was astonishingly changed' (pp.29-30)
source url: https://archive.org/details/memoirsofliterar05manc (Memoirs Lit & Phil Soc Manchester vol. 5 pt 1, 1798, scan + OCR text)
notes: Ellipsis hides 'not having then any blue in it, but'; that is fair. The flower was the 'Geranium zonale', seen 'in the Autumn of 1792' (p.29). Note the date: see NEW-2.

deciding quote: 'they all agreed, that the colour was not materially different from what it was by day-light, except my brother who saw it in the same light as myself' (p.30)
source url: https://archive.org/details/memoirsofliterar05manc (Memoirs Lit & Phil Soc Manchester vol. 5 pt 1, 1798, scan + OCR text)
notes: He 'requested some of my friends', i.e. a few friends, not 'everyone' (see NEW-1).

deciding quote: 'The face of a laurel-leaf (Prunus Lauro-cerasus) is a good match to a stick of red sealing-wax' (p.34)
source url: https://archive.org/details/memoirsofliterar05manc (Memoirs Lit & Phil Soc Manchester vol. 5 pt 1, 1798, scan + OCR text)
notes: Same sentence: 'the back of the leaf answers to the lighter red of wafers'.

deciding quote: 'OHN DALTON, passing a shop-window in Kendal, saw a pair of stockings ... "They're as red as a cherry, John!" But John could not see this, nor could brother Jonathan' (pp.99-100)
source url: https://archive.org/details/worthiescumberl02lonsgoog (Lonsdale, Worthies of Cumberland: John Dalton, preface dated 20 July 1874)
suggested wording: A story told decades later by his biographer Henry Lonsdale (1874): Dalton bought his mother stockings that looked dark to him; she said they were 'as red as a cherry', and only his brother Jonathan agreed with John.
notes: Lonsdale tells it as fact with no source; he does not say it is a family story. Calling it a 'family story' adds a source we cannot show; credit it to Lonsdale and keep the hedge ('the story goes'). He saw them as 'a bluish dark drab'. Lonsdale also dates Dalton's awareness to 'the summer of 1793', which conflicts with Dalton's own 'Autumn of 1792', a further reason to keep it hedged.

deciding quote: 'one of the humours of my eye ... is a coloured medium, probably some modification of blue. I suppose it must be the vitreous humour' (p.43)
source url: https://archive.org/details/memoirsofliterar05manc (Memoirs Lit & Phil Soc Manchester vol. 5 pt 1, 1798, scan + OCR text)
notes: He says it of 'my eye, and of the eyes of my fellows'.

deciding quote: Hunt 1995: 'He instructed that his eyes should be examined after his death'. Henry p.25: examination made 'in conformity with his strongly expressed wish'
notes: True, but no source dates the request, and it is NOT in the 1794/1798 paper. The paper says only that a tinted humour 'might be discovered by inspection, which has not been done' (p.43). The outline places it in the 1794 talk: see NEW-3.

deciding quote: 'in the beginning of the Year 1666 ... I procured me a Triangular glass-Prisme ... having darkened my chamber, and made a small hole in my window-shuts'
suggested wording: In the outline: 'By his own account, in 1666, Newton darkened his room...'
notes: Newton's own account, written in 1672. On screen, credit the date to him ('he later wrote') rather than present 1666 as an established date.

deciding quote: Letter dated 'from Cambridge, Febr. 6. 1671/72'; Phil. Trans. No. 80 (19 Feb. 1671/72), pp. 3075-3087
notes: Old-style year 1671/72 = 1672.

deciding quote: 'The gradual removal of these suspitions, at length led me to the Experimentum Crucis, which was this:'

'Colours are not Qualifications of Light, derived from Refractions, or Reflections of natural Bodies (as 'tis generally believed,) but Original and connate properties, which in divers Rays are divers.'
notes: The rest of the sentence supports 'properties the light already has'. If shown on screen, use the full sentence or end the quote at 'Bodies'.

deciding quote: Britannica: Hooke 'wrote a condescending critique'; 'The correspondence dragged on until 1678'. CUL: Huygens, Hooke and Pardies 'soon engaged Newton in a wide-ranging correspondence'
notes: 'Long argument, notably with Hooke' is fair (about six years). Britannica also says 'On the whole, the paper was also well received', so do not suggest that everyone rejected it. 'Bitter' is a reasonable gloss of 'condescending' plus Newton's withdrawal, but no source here uses that word.

deciding quote: p.[90]: 'For the rays to speak properly are not coloured. In them there is nothing else than a certain power and disposition to stir up a sensation'
suggested wording: "For the rays to speak properly are not coloured." (lower-case 'rays'; the 1704 print spells it 'fpeak' with a long s)
notes: Checked against the page image (n107 = p.[90]). The 1704 text has 'rays' in lower case, so the on-screen quote should match the print. Page number p.90 confirmed.

deciding quote: Opticks Bk I Pt II: spectrum 'divided after the manner of a musical Chord'; circle split into seven parts 'proportional to the seven musical Tones or Intervals of the eight Sounds' (Prop. III, Prop. VI)
suggested wording: Exact form: 'Newton divided his seven colours in the same proportions as the seven steps of a musical scale.'
notes: Whipple: 'his spectrum of seven colours was governed by the same ratios underlying music's diatonic scale'. 'Tied to the seven notes' is acceptable shorthand, but strictly he used the seven intervals of an octave of eight sounds.

deciding quote: York Univ. demo uses a glass of water lit by a torch 'at the very edge of the counter'; it notes rainbows appear 'wherever sunlight falls on water, glass, or plastic that has a tapered shape'
suggested wording: A glass of water in direct sunlight, near the edge of a sill, can throw a small band of colours onto the floor or wall.
notes: Physically sound and widely used as a home demo, but I could not test it. Most published versions use a torch or a mirror in water. Sam must try it in a sunny window before recording, as the claim itself says.

deciding quote: Britannica: 'Died: July 27, 1844, Manchester'. Ransome (Henry p.201): 'on the 27th of July ... I was again hastily summoned, but only to behold the lifeless body'
Ransome (Henry pp.201-202): 'On the following day, an examination of the head was made' ... 'I removed them for the purpose of making a more careful examination of them at my leisure.'
suggested wording: The day after he died, the surgeon Joseph Ransome, as Dalton had asked, examined his head and removed his eyes. He studied them more closely afterwards.
notes: Settles the Colour_v1 open note. 28 July 1844 (the day after death): head examined with 'Mr. Wilson'; eyes looked at in place ('The eyes, in situ, presented no peculiarity') and removed. The humour tests and the look-through test came later, 'at my leisure' (date not given). 'Surgeon' is supported: Plarr's Lives: Ransome served 'as Surgeon to the Royal Infirmary from 1843-1866' (https://livesonline.rcseng.ac.uk/biogs/E003029b.htm). Henry calls him Dalton's 'medical attendant'.

deciding quote: 'In the other eye, the posterior part being removed ... I did not omit to place scarlet and green together ... the contrast of the colours ... was as great as ever.'
suggested wording: Optional, more exact: 'He cut away the back of the second eye and looked through it, like a lens, at scarlet and green: to his eyes the contrast was as great as ever.'
notes: The first eye was used up testing the colour of the humours; the second was used as the lens. 'Looked as they always did' is a fair paraphrase.

deciding quote: Ransome: aqueous 'perfectly pellucid and free from colour'; vitreous 'also perfectly colourless'; lens 'slightly amber-coloured, as usual in persons of advanced age'. Hunt: 'the humors were perfectly clear'
notes: Caution: Henry's own summary on p.25 says 'The vitreous humour was of a pale yellow colour', which contradicts Ransome's first-hand account. Quote Ransome (p.202), not Henry p.25. The lens was slightly amber, as is normal with age, so say 'the fluids', not 'everything in the eye'.

deciding quote: Read 31 Oct 1794 (Dalton p.28); examined July 1844 (Henry p.201)
source url: https://archive.org/details/memoirsofliterar05manc (Memoirs Lit & Phil Soc Manchester vol. 5 pt 1, 1798, scan + OCR text)

deciding quote: SMG: 'Remains of John Dalton's eyes' ... 'Object Number: Y1997.6.38' ... 'PART OF: Manchester Literary & Philosophical Society collection' ... 'Made: 1844'
notes: Science and Industry Museum blog: the eyes 'were retained by the Literary and Philosophical Society' and 'donated to the Museum of Science and Industry in 1997'. The SMG record says nothing about what form the remains take; Hektoen says 'Ransome dried and stored the eyes' (https://hekint.org/2017/01/22/john-daltons-eyes-a-history-of-the-eye-and-color-vision-part-one/). Do not describe the remains as more than 'what is left of his eyes' without a photo or record. See NEW-5 on 'jar'.

deciding quote: Hunt 1995: 'This diagnosis ... contradicts Thomas Young's belief that Dalton was a protanope.'
notes: Hunt found Dalton was a deuteranope (lacking the middle-wave pigment). The script must not leave Young's guess standing as fact; the plan to answer it in ep 2 is fine.

deciding quote: Hunt et al., Science 267:984-988, 17 Feb 1995: 'DNA extracted from his preserved eye tissue showed that Dalton was a deuteranope'
Birch 2012: 'the prevalence of deficiency in European Caucasians is about 8% in men and about 0.4% in women'
notes: The claim keeps the population, but the outline drops it: see NEW-4. Birch also gives 4%-6.5% in Chinese and Japanese men.

deciding quote: Lonsdale p.114: 'the Continental savans, and notably those of the Academy of Geneva, to designate the defect of colour-blindness "Daltonism"'. Britannica: 'known as Daltonism'
source url: https://archive.org/details/worthiescumberl02lonsgoog (Lonsdale, Worthies of Cumberland: John Dalton, preface dated 20 July 1874) ; https://www.britannica.com/biography/John-Dalton ; https://hekint.org/2017/01/22/john-daltons-eyes-a-history-of-the-eye-and-color-vision-part-one/
suggested wording: Dalton's account became so well known that colour blindness was named after him: 'Daltonism'. The name caught on especially in continental Europe.
notes: The name is real and was widely used. Hektoen credits Pierre Prevost of Geneva with the first printed use, in 1827. But 'for a century' (outline, act 7) and 'the usual name' are not supported: in English 'colour-blindness' was already in use by the 1850s (Lonsdale uses both; George Wilson's 1855 'Researches in Colour-Blindness'). Drop 'for a century'.

deciding quote: oled-info: 'The basic PenTile structure is the RGBG matrix'; 'In RGBG PenTile displays there are only two subpixels per pixel'
notes: True for phone screens in general: they light red, green and blue sub-pixels in different strengths. Caveat: many phone OLEDs share red and blue sub-pixels (PenTile), so do not say every pixel has exactly three lights; 'three kinds of tiny light' is safe. Weak source; any display-maker page would do better.

deciding quote: Dalton p.30: 'I requested some of my friends to observe the phenomenon; when I was surprised to find they all agreed, that the colour was not materially different'
source url: https://archive.org/details/memoirsofliterar05manc (Memoirs Lit & Phil Soc Manchester vol. 5 pt 1, 1798, scan + OCR text)
suggested wording: Act 1: 'His friends: no real change. Only his brother sees what he sees.'
notes: Outline act 1 says 'Everyone else: pink, both times.' Dalton asked 'some of my friends', not everyone. He reports that they saw no material change, not that they used the word 'pink' both times (he himself says 'The flower was pink').

deciding quote: Dalton p.29: 'the colour of the flower of the Geranium zonale by candle-light, in the Autumn of 1792'. Britannica: 'In 1793, he moved to Manchester'. Lonsdale p.79: 'after twelve years' residence in Kendal ... he moved to Manchester'
source url: https://archive.org/details/memoirsofliterar05manc (Memoirs Lit & Phil Soc Manchester vol. 5 pt 1, 1798, scan + OCR text) ; https://www.britannica.com/biography/John-Dalton ; https://archive.org/details/worthiescumberl02lonsgoog (Lonsdale, Worthies of Cumberland: John Dalton, preface dated 20 July 1874)
suggested wording: Act 2: 'Kendal, 1792, then Manchester. Dalton, a Quaker teacher in his twenties...'
notes: Outline act 2 sets the geranium and friends scene in 'Manchester, 1790s'. The geranium moment and the first asking of friends were in autumn 1792, a year before he moved to Manchester, so he was in Kendal (the stockings story is also set in Kendal). The fuller investigation came 'nearly two years after' (p.30), by which time he was in Manchester. The 'Manchester plan 1794' visual suits act 3, not the geranium scene.

deciding quote: Dalton p.43: 'otherwise I apprehend it might be discovered by inspection, which has not been done.' Henry p.25: examination 'in conformity with his strongly expressed wish'
source url: https://archive.org/details/memoirsofliterar05manc (Memoirs Lit & Phil Soc Manchester vol. 5 pt 1, 1798, scan + OCR text) ; https://archive.org/details/memoirsoflifesci00henruoft
suggested wording: Act 3: 'His guess: a fluid in his eye is tinted ... Only cutting open an eye could prove it. Later, he asked that his own eyes be examined after his death.'
notes: Outline act 3 puts 'His instruction: examine my eyes after I die' inside the 31 Oct 1794 talk. The paper contains no such instruction. No source checked dates the request; keep it separate from the talk.

deciding quote: Birch 2012: 'European Caucasians is about 8% in men and about 0.4% in women and between 4% and 6.5% in men of Chinese and Japanese ethnicity'
suggested wording: Act 2: 'About 8 in every 100 men of European descent have some red-green colour deficiency, and far fewer women.'
notes: Outline act 2 says 'About 8% of men today share something like it' with no population. The figure is for men of European descent; it is lower elsewhere.

deciding quote: McGill OSS (popular): 'sitting in a jar on a shelf since 1844'. Hektoen: 'Ransome dried and stored the eyes'. SMG record: no container described
suggested wording: If no primary or museum confirmation: 'The answer waited, in what was left of his eyes, for 151 years.' Act 7 title: 'What was left'.
notes: Outline act 1 ('waited in a jar for 151 years') and act 7 ('The jar', 'the jar talks'). Only a popular secondary source says jar; the museum record and Ransome do not. Hektoen says the eyes were dried. Check the SMG object photo or ask the museum before using 'jar' as fact or showing an AI-made jar.

deciding quote: Ransome (Henry pp.202-203): Brewster 'agreed with me, that the imperfection of Dalton's vision arose from some deficient sensorial or perceptive power, rather than from any peculiarity in the eye itself.'
suggested wording: Act 6: '...A 50-year theory is wrong. The best Ransome and Sir David Brewster could say was that the fault lay in some "sensorial or perceptive power", not in the eye's fluids.'
notes: Outline act 6 says 'nobody can say what was different'. Close, but they did offer a verdict: the problem was in sensing or perception. It also makes the join to act 7 ('the difference must be in the eye's sensing itself') a sourced point.

deciding quote: Opticks p.[90]: 'In them there is nothing else than a certain power and disposition to stir up a sensation of this or that Colour'
notes: Outline act 5: 'Colour is a sensation in the one who looks' is a fair paraphrase.

deciding quote: Dalton p.29: 'I became pretty well acquainted with the theory of light and colours'; p.43: bodies 'placed in homogeneal light of any colour, appear of that particular colour'
source url: https://archive.org/details/memoirsofliterar05manc (Memoirs Lit & Phil Soc Manchester vol. 5 pt 1, 1798, scan + OCR text)
notes: Outline act 5: 'On Newton's terms, Dalton's blue-filter idea made sense.' This is interpretation; Dalton's p.43 argument is Newtonian (filtering rays). Fine as the narrator's view.

deciding quote: RMG: 'Dr Dalton, F.R.S. President of the Literary & Philosophical Society Manchester'; creators incl. James Lonsdale, Charles Turner; 'Mezzotint'; 1 October 1834
notes: Outline act 2 'Turner mezzotint' exists (1834, Charles Turner, after James Lonsdale). It shows Dalton aged about 68, not in his twenties: label it as later, or use it only with 'later famous'. 'Manchester plan 1794' not checked (visual asset).

deciding quote: Henry p.25 / Hunt: examination after death at his wish; Ransome p.201: died 27 July
notes: Outline act 6 'As he asked' and the date are fine. 'Removes the back of one' is fine (it was the second eye).
